findings.description: The policy grants ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, and cloudwatch:* on Resource "*", giving this user full control over compute, storage, and serverless resources across the entire account. A leaked or compromised deploy credential would allow an attacker to exfiltrate data, modify or destroy infrastructure, and pivot to other services. Permissions should be scoped to the specific actions and resource ARNs the deployment actually requires.

The policy is attached to a long-lived IAM user with an access key rather than a role, so the wildcard permissions are permanently available to anyone holding the static key. Combined with the unrestricted actions above, this greatly increases the blast radius and lifetime of a credential compromise.

The secret access key for this user is stored in Terraform state as encrypted_secret, and it is surfaced again in the output "svc_deploy_key_material". Terraform state and outputs are commonly stored in remote backends with broad read access, so the effective credential (decryptable with the PGP key or via console reset workflows) can leak to anyone who can read state. Long-lived static keys should be avoided in favor of IAM roles or credential rotation.

This output exposes the access key secret material and is not marked sensitive, so it is printed in plan/apply logs and displayed in CI output. Anyone with access to the pipeline logs or Terraform state can obtain the credential.
